task: Review this upper-elementary response to an original classroom poem and return it unchanged if it is useful and supported. The class has discussed how a poem can give objects wishes and can follow the distinction between quotation and interpretation. Preserve the exact line and the student's qualified reading. A short literary explanation needs neither numerical evidence nor a compulsory opposing paragraph. Do not simplify solely because of the educational label.
input: The line “The door said wait; the path said come” gives the door and the path different wishes. They do not speak aloud in the poem. I read their disagreement as a way to show the speaker's hesitation, not as proof that either choice is right.

facts.text: The supplied original poem line is exactly “The door said wait; the path said come”.
The poem presents a speaker considering whether to leave; it contains no scene of objects making audible speech.
The packet supplies no final choice or statement that staying or leaving is the correct decision.

forbidden_additions: A literal talking-door scene or invented ending
A declaration that the author certainly endorses one choice
A demand for numerical proof of the literary reading
preserve: The door said wait; the path said come
I read their disagreement as a way to show the speaker's hesitation
